p: Pavel turned up in the lobby with a crate of adapters he'd built over two weekends, and the team turned it into real changes instead.
Tamarack will rebuild the rack to plug into HEARTH, and ICD revision B, signed on a workbench in Frederick, matched on all four lines.
The rack now reaches FRO in week twenty six, and Tiago will build around a steel stand-in until it does.
Amara's card, SIX WEEKS LATE, FOUR PEOPLE OUT, is still in Nadia's badge holder.
Driving home from Frederick, she counted thirteen weeks since she'd told her father she'd come down soon.
Frank Brooks. Nadia's father. He toured the high bay with one hand pocketed.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He still tells the 2019 hatch seal story.
Odette. Safety engineer. She writes HEARTH's hazard reports.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model, and timed how long the notices waited.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She told four hundred people six weeks.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He's building around a stand-in rack.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She signed a priced change for ground commands.

Her father, Frank, called Sunday night, a little after eight. That was the hour she called Callie now, most Sundays since week five, and Callie put Rosie on and handed the phone to him last if he was still up. Tonight he called first.

On Saturday Nadia had texted him a photo from the test cell: HEARTH's forward hatch bolted to Tiago's stand, bare aluminum with blue tape on its edges, the first piece of the module that looked like it was going to space. He hadn't texted back. He had it open now. She could tell, because he talked the way he read the paper, a few words and then a stop.
That black ring. Around the door. That rubber?
Silicone. It's the seal for the hatch.
Fifteen years, she told him. HEARTH was built for fifteen. I didn't ask about the can, he said. I asked about the ring.
She didn't know. She said Brannock, the company that molded it, would have data. He made the noise he made at the TV when a weatherman said a front might stall.

Our gloves had a date on the cuff, he said. Stamped in. Every six months back to the shop for testing, worn or not. Rubber goes bad in a hot truck. The TV went quiet on his end. Mornings, you'd roll them up tight from the cuff, so the air's caught in the fingers, and hold them up by your ear.
Even if you'd checked them the day before?
Then especially. He stopped there. It was as close as he came, most years, to the year he quit climbing, and she knew better than to lean on it.

When he came back it was in his Rosie voice. Rosie had drawn a second door on the purple rocket, at the back, because Callie had told her Nadia was putting one in. She wants to know when you're coming to see it.
The weekend after the critical design review, Nadia said. I'll text you the date.
Text it now. She did, with him still on the line. He read it out loud and said okay. It didn't sound like the other times.

After he'd hung up she opened the photo again and spread it with two fingers until the seal filled the screen: a thin black line pressed into a groove, the only thing between the cabin and whatever was on the other side of that door on the day somebody shut it. She'd checked the hatch's drawings, its loads and its open time. She'd never once asked how old the rubber would be on the day it mattered.

The radio was in. On Saturday Colleen took the blue and white airplane up for the first time as its owner, with Nadia in the right seat. Before she untied it she pulled a laminated card from her flight bag and went down it out loud: the ceiling and visibility she'd fly in, the crosswind she'd land in, how much sleep she'd had, how long since she'd flown this kind of airplane. Most lines had a number. Two were close today, and she said so.
The card isn't for good days, she said. It's for the day I want to go.

Colleen's card had a small grid in one corner, four squares by four. Down the side, how likely. Across the bottom, how bad. Ice is unlikely today, she said, tapping the worst column. It's also the one that kills you. So it still gets a look.
Ice was the one she had a plan for. The freezing level was well above the route, and if the cloud tops climbed she'd turn around at the reservoir. She named the reservoir before they taxied.

Climbing out of Erie, Colleen kept glancing at the temperature and the dew point. Seven degrees apart on the ground, five over Boulder. When those two close up, the fog comes, she said. The fog's the result. The spread is the warning.
On the way back Colleen pointed out the fields she'd use if the engine stopped, one after another, without being asked.

Monday of week fifteen Nadia opened HEARTH's risk register. Amara had started it on the program's first day. It had thirty one lines, most of them cost and schedule, and eleven said owner TBD. The newest was two months old, with one exception.

The exception was a line Jun had added on Friday, after he went looking for the aft node and didn't find it: a watch item, Nadia as owner, triggered if Halo's next assembly plan stopped showing the node. It should have been there for a month.

Osprey, a company building a smaller station, had asked for proposals on a habitat module. FRO's board would decide in two weeks whether to bid, and Amara wanted HEARTH's register current before the board looked at it. There was nothing on it about the hatch. Before she did anything else she typed one line of her own, the question her father had asked on Sunday: if the seal compound ages faster than its data shows, then the hatch may not hold its leak rate late in the module's life. Owner, N. Brooks. Then she looked at the other thirty one.

It takes Monday afternoon. They go element by element, then interface by interface, with Odette's hazard reports open and Wes's old programs on the table. Fourteen new lines go up, each written as if this, then that. At the hatch Wes reads her line off the screen and says the compound has flown for twenty years. She leaves it up.

Tuesday a test cell technician named Gus caught Nadia at the coffee urn. He'd been at FRO since the cargo days, and he'd read Nadia's seal line on the HEARTH room screen Monday, on his way through with a cart. His was one of the six names on the lockout tags by the cell's valve panel. He waited until the urn was empty.

That 2019 seal, he said. Wes tells it like he caught a bad seal. He did. He also put it in. We'd bought seals for two modules and the second one got canceled, so the spare sat in a bag in the cage for two years. Wes used it because it was there. He refilled his cup. I wasn't going to say that with him at the table.

She asks Gus if she can put his name on it. He says fine, as long as she tells Wes herself. Nadia goes to Wes's desk before lunch and tells him what she's adding and who it came from. Wes looks at the 2019 photo over his desk for a while. It was my call to buy for two, he says. Put it on. At Thursday's review the leads speak last, and Gus and two other technicians add three lines before Wes says anything.

Wednesday they rated the new lines. FRO's scales were Amara's, from the first day, and they were good ones: five levels each, a probability band behind every likelihood, and a cost, a schedule slip, a performance loss and a crew safety effect behind every consequence.

The seal took longest. Brannock Seal, in Ohio, had molded the compound for twenty years, and its published aging data covered the equivalent of ten. HEARTH was built for fifteen. One FRO seal had failed before, after two years in a bag. If the seal let go in the module's later years, the hatch wouldn't hold when the crew needed it shut. Finding that out on the ground meant new seals, both hatches reworked and the testing done again.
Likelihood one, Wes said. It's flown for twenty years.

Likelihood three: data for ten of fifteen years, and one failure of the same kind at FRO. Consequence four: a hatch that fails its leak rate means rework and retest, and a hatch that won't hold when it's needed. Nadia writes the basis under both numbers. Wes reads it and doesn't argue with the ten.

Thursday the seal came back to the HEARTH room with a rating on it and four ideas. Wes wanted to stop worrying about rubber altogether. Amara wanted Brannock to own it. Odette wanted the risk lower before anyone called it handled. Lower first, she said. Then we can use the word.

Tiago pointed out that the hatch would be leak tested twice before it shipped, once in qualification and once as flight hardware, and that a bad seal would show. Nadia felt the pull of that one. Two leak tests. Two green passes.

Brannock agrees to age samples from HEARTH's lot to a fifteen year equivalent, with results in week twenty four. Its routine aging test on the same lot ends sooner, the day after the board votes. Jun finds a second compound from another maker and orders samples. Odette signs off on the plan, not the risk.

Monday of week sixteen Jun pulled Brannock's certificates for the compound's last four lots from receiving. Each showed the same test. Samples were aged in an oven, squeezed flat for a set time, then measured for how much they failed to spring back. That was compression set, and Brannock's limit was 25 percent. HEARTH's own lot, molded the week before, was in Brannock's oven now. Its result would come at the end of next week.
Brannock Seal certificates, last four lots. Compression set after aging, oldest to newest: 14, 16, 19 and 22 percent. Limit 25 percent. All four PASS.

Jun plots the four points and draws the limit across the top. Nadia sets the threshold at 20 percent, where there's still room to act. The last lot is already past it. She writes to Brannock that afternoon and asks what changed. Brannock's quality manager answers that every lot passed. She asks again.
Tuesday Jun put the seal's line up on the screen in the HEARTH room. Its number on the register was R-032.

HEARTH risk register, R-032, hatch seal. Risk: if the seal compound ages faster than its ten years of data show, then both hatches may not hold their leak rate late in the module's fifteen year life.. Owner: N. Brooks. Likelihood 3, consequence 4.. Basis: aging data covers ten years. One earlier FRO seal failed in 2019, after two years in storage. Brannock's lot results are trending up.

The handling Odette had signed off on had three dated steps: Brannock's routine result on HEARTH's lot at the end of next week, a qualified backup compound a few weeks after that, and the fifteen year aging result in week twenty four.
Amara wants the date it goes green, Jun said. I told her I'd ask you, so she'd stop asking me.

Jun draws it from today's score: one step for each dated action, each down to the rating it should reach if it works, and a second line for what really happens. Amara looks for the week it goes green. And if a step fails? Then the line goes up, and we see it the week it does.

Wednesday Tiago drove up to Frederick to look at the rack, because the agreement still gave FRO no better way to see it. Irena walked him to the whiteboard at the end of the clean room. She'd moved the magnets herself.
He came back with a photo. Eight of the twenty packages were green. The forecast from two weeks back, two a week, said nine by now.

The integration plan had been rebuilt twice since the rack first slipped. It read now the way it should have from the start: Tamarack's stand-in first, the real rack three weeks later, and the ship date moving only if the rack slipped past week twenty eight.
Amara saw the photo before Nadia did. One package behind, she said. Do I call Pavel?

Nadia works it with Amara over the photo. Twelve left at two a week, so Tamarack finishes about two weeks before its test chamber frees up. The chamber's the real clock. The rack still lands in week twenty six, with about a week and a half of float, and that's nowhere near the trigger. She logs the variance and the float. Amara doesn't call Pavel.
Thursday Tiago called her down to the test cell. He had the cell's schedule on the whiteboard by the valve panel, where the six lockout tags still hung.

The week after next, the forward hatch's qualification article went into the chamber for its leak test: three days to pump down, hold and measure, and bring it back up. Three weeks after that the seal fixture went in for its own leak test, a steel ring with the hatch's groove cut into it, and that was three more days. After that the cell was booked solid with the aft hatch.

The fixture fits on the hatch stand, he said. He'd already measured it. Same chamber, same helium, separate lines so the two leaks don't mix. One pumpdown. I get three days back, and I don't burn a second helium charge. The fixture has to be built and leak checked by the end of next week, or it doesn't work.

She writes it with him at the whiteboard. Opportunity: shared pumpdown. Owner: Tiago. Benefit: three days of cell time and a helium charge. Must be true: the fixture built and leak checked by Friday of next week, separate measurement lines, and both procedures still meeting their own objectives. Trigger: if the fixture isn't ready that Friday, both tests run separately as planned. Tiago initials it. I'd have done it anyway, he says. Now I'll know when to stop.
Friday Helen called about the seal. Halo's crew office read every hazard report FRO sent, and Odette's report for losing hatch isolation now pointed at the seal.
The day that seal matters is the day somebody shuts that hatch because something's wrong on one side of it, Helen said. Suppose it's tired by then. Year twelve, say. What does my crew do?

It turns into three things. A leak check the crew can run across the shut hatch in ten minutes. A procedure for keeping the hatch shut on a weak seal while the station tops up the air. And a spare seal on board with its tools, so the crew can change it from the cabin side, which Wes says he can design for if he knows now. Helen asks for the ten minutes in writing.

Monday of week seventeen Amara came to Nadia's desk with a note from the chair of FRO's board. Osprey's request was real: one habitat module for a smaller station, proposals due in five weeks. The board would vote on Thursday. Before it voted, the chair wanted to know whether HEARTH was healthy enough to bet a second module on, and she'd asked for one number: the count of red risks.
I've stood on that crate with bad news once this year, Amara said. I'd like to stand on it and say we're bidding on something.

Nadia gives Amara four lines instead of a count, each with a threshold: the burn-down of each top risk against its plan, the share of handling actions done on time, the predicted egress margins, and Tamarack's packages against forecast. Amara stops at the second line and asks which of these would have warned her about the rack. Actions on time. Pavel's would have been late by week ten. Amara is quiet a moment. I'd have liked week ten.
Tuesday Amara built the board's deck. HEARTH's five highest risks went on one slide. At a twelve, the seal was one of the five.
Wes came in while she was arranging it. Brannock's result on our lot comes Friday, he said. If it passes, the seal comes off that slide. Don't put my hatch in front of the board for three days.
Amara looked at Nadia. It would be one meeting with good news in it, she said. She didn't say it like an order.

The seal stays on the slide, one line, the same as on the register: the rating, the handling, the result due Friday, and the cost if the lot fails. Wes reads it without a word. An hour later he sends Nadia the 2019 leak report, scanned, with no note.

The board met Thursday afternoon in the conference room over the lobby: seven people, Amara at the screen, and Nadia in a chair by the wall, because the chair of the board had asked for HEARTH's systems engineer by title.

Osprey wanted a module like HEARTH, a little smaller, in two years. Building it would need FRO's high bay, its test cell and the people who had built HEARTH so far, while HEARTH was still being built.
The chair stopped on the risk slide, at the seal. Friday, she said. And if it fails? Amara told her what it would cost.
Then the chair turned to the wall. Ms. Brooks. Can FRO build two of these at once?

She does it in four minutes. Wes and Tiago can't move before HEARTH's critical design review, the test cell is full through week thirty, and a bid could reuse HEARTH's design and start from its risk register. The board votes to bid, with its own team, HEARTH first in the test cell, and a go or no go before the proposal goes out. When the vote is done Nadia takes the card out of her badge holder, SIX WEEKS LATE, FOUR PEOPLE OUT, and slides it down the table. Amara writes the three conditions on the back and hands it back to her.
Brannock's email came in at twenty to four on Friday.

An email from Brannock Seal, Quality. Subject: Lot hold, HEARTH hatch seal compound. Nadia, Wes,. The lot molded for HEARTH failed lot acceptance today. After accelerated aging, compression set was 31 percent against our 25 percent limit. Retained samples retested at 30 percent. The lot is on hold, including both hatch seals, the two spares, and the two fixture samples we sent early for fit. We're looking at what changed in our process this year. You'll have first findings next week.. Brannock Quality

Amara forwarded it to the board's chair within ten minutes, with two lines of her own: the seal result we discussed yesterday, failed; handling under way, cost and schedule by Wednesday. The chair answered from her phone. Understood. The bid conditions stand.

Nadia went down to the test cell. Tiago had the seal fixture on the bench beside the hatch stand, finished and leak checked that morning for Monday's pumpdown, a steel ring with a black seal pressed into its groove. The trigger on his opportunity had a date on it, and the date was today. The fixture was ready. The seal wasn't.
She read the lot number off the traveler tag wired to the fixture and checked it against the email. Same lot as both flight seals, still sitting in Ohio.

Tiago opened the drawer under the valve panel, where the lockout tags were kept, and took out a red one printed HOLD. He wrote the lot number on it and held out the pen. It's your line on the register, he said. Same rule as the lockouts. Your name goes on it, and only you take it off. She wrote her name.
Under it she wrote the date, the way the date had been stamped on her father's gloves. She hung the tag on the fixture's valve and squared it on its wire.

Wes came down while she was doing it. He looked at the tag. Then he ran his thumb around the seal in its groove, all the way around, the way he'd been seating them for thirty years. In 2019 I put mine in myself, and I found it the week it shipped, he said. This is week seventeen. He went back up the stairs. A minute later she could hear him on the phone to Ohio.

Upstairs she changed the seal's line on the register from a risk to an issue, and Jun's burn-down redrew itself. The step down that was due this week went the other way. The line went up the week it happened, the way she'd told Amara it would.
